notes.meaning: Rehoboam traveled north to Shechem because the northern tribes had gathered there to crown him as king. Shechem was an ancient, central meeting place in the territory of Ephraim, far from Jerusalem. The northern leaders met there so they could negotiate freely with their new ruler before pledging their allegiance.

Jeroboam heard about the gathering while he was still living in exile in Egypt. He had fled there to escape King Solomon, who had tried to kill him after a prophet promised Jeroboam ten tribes. Now that Solomon had died, the path was open for Jeroboam to return.

The northern leaders invited Jeroboam to join their assembly and speak for them before Rehoboam. Because Jeroboam had high standing and a bold reputation, the people believed he would give them greater leverage. Together, the delegation approached Rehoboam to present their demands before crowning him.

The people asked Rehoboam to lighten the heavy load of forced labor and high taxes that Solomon had placed on them. Solomon had required immense resources to build his palaces, fortresses, and magnificent court. The assembly promised to serve the new king faithfully if he showed mercy and eased their burden.

Rehoboam asked for three days to think about their request before giving an answer, and the people agreed to leave. Taking time to deliberate was customary when making major royal decisions. However, this delay gave the unhappy assembly time to organize and prepare for what might happen next.

Rehoboam first asked for guidance from the elder statesmen who had served as counselors to his father Solomon. These men had decades of experience in ruling and had learned from the wisdom of Solomon's early reign. Rehoboam asked them directly how he should answer the people's plea.

The elders urged Rehoboam to act as a servant to the people by speaking kindly and granting their request. They explained that a true king leads by caring for his subjects rather than ruling harshly over them. If he showed them kindness and humility today, the people would gladly serve him for the rest of his life.

Rehoboam ignored the wise counsel of the older advisers and went instead to the young men of his own generation. These younger men had grown up with him in royal luxury and lacked practical experience in governing a nation. The king preferred their company because his own pride resisted humbling himself before his subjects.

Rehoboam asked his peers what answer they thought he should send back to the assembly. By restating the people's request to make the yoke lighter, he invited the young men to help him push back. He was looking for advice that matched his own desire to show authority rather than offer relief.

The young advisers told Rehoboam to answer the assembly with extreme arrogance. They suggested he tell them that his little finger was thicker than his father's waist, an idiom meaning he possessed far greater power and resolve than Solomon ever had. They wanted him to crush any spirit of protest with sheer intimidation.

The young men urged the king to promise harsher labor and harsher punishments than his father had ever imposed. While Solomon used ordinary whips to enforce discipline, Rehoboam promised to use scorpions, which were scourges loaded with sharp metal barbs. This cruel boast was meant to terrify the people into absolute submission.

Jeroboam and the assembly returned on the third day just as Rehoboam had instructed. The people showed patience and gave the new king a full opportunity to respond reasonably to their petition. They stood ready to hear whether their future held relief or further oppression.

Rehoboam gave the people a harsh and threatening answer instead of a peaceful one. He completely cast aside the moderation and gentle words recommended by his father's older advisers. In his foolish pride, he chose to bully the assembly rather than win their hearts.

The king repeated the exact words suggested by his young companions, threatening to make their burdens far heavier. He told the assembly that if his father beat them with whips, he would punish them with painful, barbed scourges. This insulting response convinced the northern tribes that Rehoboam would be a ruthless tyrant.

Rehoboam refused to listen to the people because God was orchestrating these events behind the scenes. Years earlier, the Lord had announced through the prophet Ahijah that ten tribes would be torn away as judgment for Solomon's idolatry. God permitted Rehoboam's foolish pride and bad decisions to bring about this promised consequence.

differ.view: God sovereignly directed circumstances and gave Rehoboam over to his own foolish heart to fulfill His predetermined decree, without being the author of sin.
God did not cause Rehoboam's cruelty or foolishness; the Lord used the turning of political events to bring judgment while leaving human free will intact.

notes.meaning: When the northern tribes heard the king's harsh refusal, they renounced all loyalty to the royal family of David. They shouted an old rallying cry, telling the house of David to look after its own tribe while they returned to their homes. The long-standing union between the northern tribes and Judah was shattered in a single day.

Although the northern tribes broke away, Rehoboam still ruled over the people living within the territory of Judah. This included members of other tribes who had settled in southern towns or remained loyal to the sanctuary in Jerusalem. The grand united kingdom was now reduced to a smaller southern realm.

Rehoboam sent Adoram, his officer in charge of forced labor, to bring the northern tribes back under control or collect taxes. Sending the very man who represented their heavy burdens only enraged the people, and they stoned him to death. Realizing his own life was in danger, Rehoboam quickly jumped into his chariot and fled to Jerusalem.

The northern tribes remained in permanent rebellion against the dynasty of David from that time onward. What began as a dispute over taxes and forced labor ended in a lasting national divide. The writer notes that this separation continued down through the history of both nations.

When the northern tribes learned that Jeroboam had returned, they called a national assembly and crowned him king over Israel. Ten tribes joined together to form this new northern kingdom, fulfilling what God had spoken through Ahijah. Only the tribe of Judah, along with neighboring Benjamin, remained loyal to David's line.

Back in Jerusalem, Rehoboam gathered 180,000 elite warriors from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin to reclaim the northern tribes by force. He was determined to launch a civil war to restore the united kingdom under his rule. His southern followers stood ready to march and fight on his behalf.

Before the army could march out, God sent a message through the prophet Shemaiah, who is called a man of God. This title shows that Shemaiah was a recognized messenger who spoke with the Lord's authority. God intervened directly to stop the brother-against-brother war before it began.

Shemaiah was ordered to deliver God's message to King Rehoboam, to the warriors of Judah and Benjamin, and to all the remaining people. The warning was addressed to every level of society so that no one would be confused about God's will. It reminded the king and his army that they were under divine command.

God commanded the army not to fight against their Israelite brothers because the division of the kingdom had been determined by Him. To their credit, Rehoboam and his soldiers obeyed the Lord and disbanded their forces to return home in peace. Submitting to God's word prevented a bloody civil war.

Jeroboam established his royal capital by fortifying Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and he lived there. He also fortified Penuel, a strategic outpost east of the Jordan River along major trade routes. These building projects strengthened the military defenses of his new northern kingdom.

In his private thoughts, Jeroboam began to worry that the kingdom would eventually slip away and return to David's descendants. Instead of trusting God's promise to establish his house if he remained faithful, he relied on human calculations and fear. His political anxiety led him to question God's protection.

Jeroboam worried that if his subjects traveled to the temple in Jerusalem for religious feasts, their loyalty would shift back to Rehoboam. He feared that the beauty of temple worship and old shared memories would turn their hearts against him. In his mind, keeping his people away from Jerusalem was a matter of political survival.

After consulting his advisers, Jeroboam made two golden calves and told the people that traveling all the way to Jerusalem was too difficult. He presented the statues as the gods who had led Israel out of Egypt, deliberately echoing Aaron's words at Mount Sinai. He invented a convenient, counterfeit religion to keep his subjects from visiting Judah.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars propose that Jeroboam did not intend to introduce foreign gods, but meant the golden calves as pedestals or thrones for the invisible God, similar to the cherubim in Jerusalem.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Catholic teaching views the calves as symbolic representations of Yahweh that Jeroboam used to lead Israel into a tragic religious schism alongside their political separation.

notes.meaning: Jeroboam set up one golden calf at Bethel in the south and the other at Dan in the far north. Bethel sat right near the southern border, intercepting travelers heading toward Jerusalem, and had holy associations from the time of Jacob. Dan served the northern territory and had already been a center for unauthorized worship for centuries.

This new worship system became a great national sin that led the entire nation into spiritual ruin. The people eagerly embraced the convenience and traveled all the way to Dan to worship before the calf. By replacing God's true sanctuary with golden idols, the kingdom turned away from the Lord.

Jeroboam built shrines on pagan high places and appointed priests from any family, completely ignoring the law of Moses. God's law required that only men from the tribe of Levi could serve as priests at His altar. By creating his own priesthood from the common people, Jeroboam broke God's explicit commands.

Jeroboam also established an annual festival in the eighth month to imitate the Feast of Tabernacles held in Judah during the seventh month. He went up to the altar he had built in Bethel to offer sacrifices to the golden calves and stationed his new priests there. By copying the genuine holy day on a date of his own choice, he gave his false religion an appearance of authenticity.

On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, a date he invented out of his own imagination, Jeroboam offered sacrifices on the altar at Bethel. He burned incense and led the festival himself, acting as both king and high priest. This self-made religion set the northern kingdom on a path of idolatry that ultimately brought about its downfall.
